challenges.name: pii-redaction-quiz
challenges.title: Read the redacted logs
challenges.description: Two pieces of evidence from the grading assistant's log pipeline: a one-line regex for national ID numbers, and a redacted trace of a prompt and its output.

questions.question:
The log shipper redacts national ID numbers (12 digits) with:

line = line.replace(/\b\d{12}\b/g, "[NATIONAL_ID]");

Input line:
2026-10-27T09:15:42Z appeal sub-202610270915 learner_cccd=079203001234 course=course_204512345678

Statement: "On this line the regex redacts the learner's national ID and nothing else."
questions.explanation: False. \b is a boundary between a word character (letters, digits, _) and a non-word character. "-" is not a word character, so there is a boundary between "sub-" and "202610270915", and the submission id is redacted too: the line becomes "appeal sub-[NATIONAL_ID] learner_cccd=[NATIONAL_ID]". The course id survives only because "_" is a word character, so there is no boundary between "course_" and the digits. The two ids are now indistinguishable from the learner's ID, and the submission can no longer be found from the log. The misconception is that \b means "a whole token"; state the characters that may not touch the match (for example letters, digits, "_" and "-") with lookbehind and lookahead instead, and test the rule on real ids from your logs.

questions.question:
A span of the grading assistant after redaction with consistent pseudonyms per document (one trace = one document):

prompt: "Grade the submission of [NAME_1] ([EMAIL_1]). Rubric: ... Submission: ... # reviewed with [NAME_2]"
output: "Great work, [NAME_1]! A copy of this feedback was sent to [EMAIL_1]."
counts: { EMAIL: 2, NAME: 3, PHONE: 0, NATIONAL_ID: 0 }

Statement: "From this redacted span alone, an engineer can tell that the model repeated the learner's email address in its output."
questions.explanation: True. Consistent pseudonyms give the same value the same placeholder within one document, so [EMAIL_1] in the output is the same address as [EMAIL_1] in the prompt, and the counts confirm two email occurrences. The engineer sees that the model echoed personal data into learner-facing text (a bug worth a guardrail) without seeing the address itself. A redaction that replaced everything with a bare "[REDACTED]" would hide exactly this. The misconception is that redaction must destroy all structure; it only has to remove the values. Note that the numbering restarts in every document, so [EMAIL_1] is not a user id that can be joined across traces - which is the point.

challenges.name: redact-personal-data
challenges.title: Redact personal data before logging
challenges.description:
Last week a trace export of the CodeDev grading assistant showed learner emails, phone numbers and full names in the stored prompts. Write redact(text, roster), which runs on every prompt and model output before it is logged. Input (JSON): { roster: string[] (the full names of the course's learners and reviewers), text: string }. Output: { text, counts }.

Process the types in this order, each on the text left by the previous one, finding non-overlapping matches from left to right:
1. EMAIL: [A-Za-z0-9._%+-]+@[A-Za-z0-9-]+(\.[A-Za-z0-9-]+)+. Two emails are the same value when their lowercase forms are equal.
2. NATIONAL_ID: exactly 12 consecutive digits (the citizen ID number). Same value = same digits.
3. PHONE (Vietnamese): "+84" or "0", followed by 9 digits; each of those 9 digits may be preceded by one space or one dot. Examples: 0912345678, 0912 345 678, 091.234.5678, +84912345678, +84 912 345 678. Same value = "0" + the 9 digits, so +84 912 345 678 and 0912.345.678 are one phone.
   A NATIONAL_ID or PHONE match must not have a letter (A-Z, a-z), a digit, "_" or "-" immediately before or after it. This keeps platform ids and times intact: course ids such as course_079203001234, submission ids such as sub-202610270915, lesson ids such as lesson-lle-2-3, ISO timestamps such as 2026-10-27T09:15:42.120Z and epoch milliseconds such as 1793025136120 (13 digits) are not personal data.
4. NAME: a full name from the roster, matched case-insensitively and diacritic-insensitively. Normalisation (fold): s.normalize("NFD"), remove the characters U+0300 to U+036F, replace "đ" with "d" and "Đ" with "D", then toLowerCase(). The text and the roster are in NFC, so every character folds to exactly one character and position i of the folded text is position i of the text. Trim each roster entry and ignore empty ones; entries that fold to the same string are the same person (one value). A name matches at position i when its folded form equals the folded text there and the folded characters just before and just after it (if any) are not a-z or 0-9 (so "Lê An" does not match inside "Lê Anh"). When several names match at the same position, take the longest.

Replace each match with [TYPE_k], where k numbers the distinct values of that type in order of first appearance (1, 2, ...) and the same value always gets the same k in this document. Everything else in the text stays exactly as it was. counts has the keys EMAIL, NATIONAL_ID, PHONE and NAME with the number of replaced occurrences (0 when none). Texts are up to 50 KB with up to 100 roster entries.
hints: What makes two occurrences "the same value" for each type? Write that key down per type (lowercase email, the 9 digits after the prefix, the folded name) before you write any regex - the numbering and the counts follow from it.

Look at three places: a Map from type plus key to its number, filled in order of first appearance; the characters around each number match (lookbehind (?<!...) and lookahead (?!...) do this in one regex, \b does not, because it treats "-" as a boundary); and for names, a folded copy of the text that you search while you copy the original characters into the result.

A worked example on other data: with the key "digits of a 6-digit ticket number", the text "T 123456, t-123456, 123 456, 123456" redacted with the rule "no letter, digit, _ or - right before or after" gives "T [TICKET_1], t-123456, 123 456, [TICKET_1]" with count 2: the hyphenated one touches "-", and the spaced one is not 6 consecutive digits.
